statement: A drawer holds 12 red socks, 10 blue socks and 8 green socks, all mixed up. You take socks out one at a time in the dark. What is the smallest number of socks you must take to be certain of having three of the same colour?

choices.misconception: I thought that one more than the number of colours must give three of a kind, which only guarantees a PAIR.
I got to two of each colour, then added one more for each colour instead of one more in total.
I assumed the worst case meant emptying the largest pile of 12 reds first.
I answered with the number of socks I want rather than the number I must take to be sure of them.

hints: Ask what the unluckiest possible draw looks like.
The worst case is taking two of every colour without ever getting a third. How many socks is that?
Two of each colour is 2 x 3 = 6 socks with no colour reaching three. The seventh sock must complete a set, so the answer is 7.

solutions.reliable: Imagine the unluckiest draw possible. You could take 2 red, 2 blue and 2 green - six socks - and still have no colour three times over. So six is not enough. But there are only three colours, so the seventh sock has to be red, blue or green, and whichever it is, that colour now has three. The answer is 7. The transferable idea: to guarantee something, work out the largest number of picks that could still fail, then add one.
solutions.elegant: Two of each colour is the largest failing draw at six socks, so seven forces success.

whyOnTest: Guarantee questions are answered by the worst case, never by the likely case, and that reversal is the whole skill.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
